title: Unit 4 In-Class Lecture
description: Unit 4 lecture deck (Sept 29): tax cuts, subsidies and the in-class $20-tax exercise, plus Market A price-control drills.

inclass.title: In-class exercise (Unit 4 lecture)
inclass.body: Demand is **P = 260 − 3Q** and supply is **P = 20 + 2Q**. Later questions add a **$20 per-unit tax on producers**, which makes supply + tax **P = 40 + 2Q**. (The lecture left these answer slides blank to work through in class.)

marketA.title: Market A (Unit 4 slides)
marketA.body: Demand is **P = 100 − 2Q** and supply is **P = 0.5Q**. With no intervention, Q* = 40 and P* = $20, so CS = $1,600, PS = $400 and total surplus = $2,000.

questions.prompt: The government **cuts** a per-unit sales tax. According to the Unit 4 lecture, what happens in that market?
options: Consumers' price falls by the full amount of the tax cut, and producers' price is unchanged
Quantity sold rises, producers' price rises, and consumers' price falls — but by less than the amount of the tax cut
Quantity sold falls, because producers now keep less of each sale
Nothing changes until something shifts the demand curve
questions.explanation: A tax cut **runs the tax process in reverse** (lecture slide 9): S + tax shifts back down, so the quantity sold **increases**, producers **raise** their price (they move up their supply curve as they sell more), and consumers pay a **lower** price — but the drop is **smaller than the tax cut**, because part of the cut goes to producers. That is the same incidence logic as a tax: the cut is split between the two sides, so (a) is wrong. (c) has the direction backwards, and (d) ignores that the tax itself shifts the supply-plus-tax curve.

questions.prompt: A **subsidy** is a payment from the government to firms that covers part of the cost of production. How does a per-unit subsidy show up on a supply-and-demand graph?
options: Demand shifts right by the subsidy amount
Supply shifts up (leftward) by the subsidy amount
Supply shifts down (rightward) by the subsidy amount — an increase in supply
Neither curve shifts; only the market price changes
questions.explanation: The subsidy **lowers the per-unit cost of production**, so at every quantity firms will accept a price lower by the subsidy amount: the supply curve shifts **down by the subsidy** (S<sub>sub</sub>), which is the same as a rightward **increase in supply** (slide 10). It is paid to firms, not buyers, so demand (a) doesn't move. (b) is what a **tax** does. (d) is wrong because a cost change is a supply shifter.

questions.prompt: Compared with the free-market outcome, what does a per-unit subsidy to producers do, according to the lecture?
options: It reduces production and raises the price consumers pay
It raises the price consumers pay, because firms now have more money to spend
It is costless to society, because the government rather than consumers pays for it
It increases production and lowers the price consumers pay, but the money must be raised by taxing other goods
questions.explanation: With supply shifted down by the subsidy, the new equilibrium has a **higher quantity** and a **lower consumer price** (slide 11). The lecture's catch: **"the money to pay for the subsidy must be raised by taxing other goods"**, so (c) is wrong. Those taxes distort other markets. (a) and (b) describe the effect of a tax or a supply decrease, the opposite shift.

questions.prompt: A long-standing per-unit subsidy is removed. What happens to price and quantity?
options: Price rises and quantity falls back to the free-market equilibrium
Price falls and quantity rises further
Both price and quantity fall below the free-market levels
Nothing — firms have already adjusted to the subsidized price
questions.explanation: Removing the subsidy **reverses the process** (slide 12). Supply shifts back up to the original S, so the consumer price **rises** and quantity **falls back to the free-market equilibrium** (P*, Q*). It returns to the free-market levels, not below them, so (c) is wrong. (b) has both directions backwards.

questions.prompt: According to the Unit 4 lecture, a free market produces the largest possible total surplus, so any government intervention in that market will reduce market efficiency.
questions.explanation: **True.** Slide 4 states it directly: *"A free market will produce the largest possible total surplus. Any intervention by the government will reduce market efficiency."* Floors, ceilings, quotas, taxes and subsidies all move quantity away from Q* and create a deadweight loss. A government may still choose one for **normative** reasons (e.g. equity), but that is a separate question from efficiency.

questions.topic: Expenditure vs. revenue under a tax
questions.prompt: Without a sales tax, consumer expenditure equals firm revenue (P × Q). After a unit tax, consumers spend P<sub>C</sub> × Q<sub>t</sub> but firms receive only P<sub>S</sub> × Q<sub>t</sub>. The gap between these two amounts equals…
options: The deadweight loss
The government's tax revenue
The consumer incidence of the tax
Producer surplus
questions.explanation: The slide's wording is careful: expenditure equals firm revenue **"in a market without sales taxes."** With a tax, the gap is (P<sub>C</sub> − P<sub>S</sub>) × Q<sub>t</sub>, and P<sub>C</sub> − P<sub>S</sub> is exactly the tax. So the gap = tax × Q<sub>t</sub> = **tax revenue**. The deadweight loss (a) is surplus on units that are *no longer traded*, so it never shows up as spending. Consumer incidence (c) is a per-unit price change (P<sub>C</sub> − P*), not a total.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. What is the free-market equilibrium quantity Q*?
questions.explanation: Set the two P equations equal: 20 + 2Q = 260 − 3Q → 5Q = 240 → **Q* = 48**.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. What is the free-market equilibrium price P*?
questions.explanation: Substitute Q* = 48 into either curve: P = 260 − 3(48) = 260 − 144 = **$116**; check with supply: 20 + 2(48) = $116 ✓.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. Before any tax, what is consumer surplus?
questions.explanation: CS = ½ × base × height = ½ × 48 × (260 − 116) = ½ × 48 × 144 = **$3,456**. The height runs from P* up to the **demand intercept** ($260).

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. Before any tax, what is producer surplus?
questions.explanation: PS = ½ × 48 × (116 − 20) = ½ × 48 × 96 = **$2,304**. Watch the height: it is P* minus the **supply intercept** ($20), not P* minus zero. Using 116 would give $2,784, a common wrong answer.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. The government adds a **$20 per-unit tax** on producers. What is the new quantity traded?
questions.explanation: **Shift:** S + tax is P = 20 + 2Q + 20 = 40 + 2Q (slide 17). **Solve:** 40 + 2Q = 260 − 3Q → 5Q = 220 → **Q<sub>t</sub> = 44**, down from 48.

questions.topic: Consumer and producer prices after a tax
questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. With the $20 tax and 44 units traded, what price do consumers pay (tax included), and what price do producers keep?
options: Consumers pay $136; producers keep $116
Consumers pay $116; producers keep $96
Consumers pay $128; producers keep $108
Consumers pay $108; producers keep $128
questions.explanation: **Split** at Q<sub>t</sub> = 44: the consumer price comes from **demand**, 260 − 3(44) = **$128**. The producer price comes from the **original supply**, 20 + 2(44) = **$108**. Check: 128 − 108 = $20 = the tax ✓. (a) adds the full tax to P*, which would mean consumers pay all of it — only true if demand were vertical. (b) subtracts the full tax from P*. (d) swaps the two prices.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. How much tax revenue does the $20 tax raise?
questions.explanation: Tax revenue = tax × quantity sold = $20 × 44 = **$880**. Use the after-tax quantity (44), not Q* (48); 20 × 48 = $960 is the classic slip.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. What is consumer surplus after the $20 tax?
questions.explanation: CS = ½ × 44 × (260 − 128) = ½ × 44 × 132 = **$2,904** (down from $3,456). The height uses the **consumer** price $128.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. What is producer surplus after the $20 tax?
questions.explanation: PS = ½ × 44 × (108 − 20) = ½ × 44 × 88 = **$1,936** (down from $2,304). The height uses the **producer** price $108, never the $128 consumers pay.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. What is the deadweight loss caused by the $20 tax?
questions.explanation: DWL = ½ × (Q* − Q<sub>t</sub>) × (P<sub>C</sub> − P<sub>S</sub>) = ½ × (48 − 44) × (128 − 108) = ½ × 4 × 20 = **$40**. Check with the slides' method, DWL = old surplus − new surplus: (3,456 + 2,304) − (2,904 + 1,936 + 880) = 5,760 − 5,720 = **$40** ✓.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. How is the $20 tax burden split between consumers and producers?
options: Consumers bear the full $20, because the tax raises the price they pay
Consumers bear $8 per unit and producers bear $12 per unit
Producers bear the full $20, because the tax is placed on producers
Consumers bear $12 per unit and producers bear $8 per unit
questions.explanation: Consumer incidence = P<sub>C</sub> − P* = 128 − 116 = **$12**; producer incidence = P* − P<sub>S</sub> = 116 − 108 = **$8**; together they equal the $20 tax ✓. Consumers bear more because demand is steeper (slope 3) than supply (slope 2): the **steeper side pays more**, and 3 ÷ (3 + 2) = 60% of $20 = $12. Who is legally charged (c) doesn't decide the burden, and the consumer price rises by **less** than the full tax (a).

questions.topic: Binding price ceiling — quantity and shortage

source.label: Unit 4 Drill · Market A
source.note: Built on Market A from the Unit 4 slides (P = 100 − 2Q, P = 0.5Q). The slides show these policies on graphs; these calculations take them one step further, the way the Ch. 4 lesson page does.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. The government sets a **price ceiling of $15**. How many units are actually sold, and what is the shortage?
options: 30 units are sold, with a shortage of 12.5 units
42.5 units are sold, with a shortage of 12.5 units
30 units are sold, with a surplus of 12.5 units
40 units are sold, because the ceiling is not binding
questions.explanation: The ceiling ($15) is **below** P* ($20), so it binds. At $15, sellers offer Q<sub>S</sub>: 15 = 0.5Q → **30**; buyers want Q<sub>D</sub>: 15 = 100 − 2Q → **42.5**. Under a price control **the short side rules**: you can't buy what isn't offered, so only **30** are sold. The **shortage** (excess demand) is 42.5 − 30 = **12.5**. (b) uses the quantity demanded as the amount sold. (c) mislabels a shortage as a surplus. (d) is wrong because a ceiling below P* is binding.

questions.topic: Deadweight loss of a price ceiling

source.label: Unit 4 Drill · Market A
source.note: Built on Market A from the Unit 4 slides (P = 100 − 2Q, P = 0.5Q). The slides show these policies on graphs; these calculations take them one step further, the way the Ch. 4 lesson page does.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. With the **$15 price ceiling** (30 units sold), what is the deadweight loss?
questions.explanation: At the 30th unit, buyers value it at the demand price 100 − 2(30) = $40, while it costs only 0.5(30) = $15 to make. DWL = ½ × (Q* − 30) × (40 − 15) = ½ × 10 × 25 = **$125**. Check: new CS = (40 − 15) × 30 + ½ × 30 × (100 − 40) = $1,650, new PS = ½ × 30 × 15 = $225, and the old total was $2,000, so DWL = 2,000 − 1,875 = $125 ✓. The height is the gap between **demand and supply at 30 units** ($40 − $15), not the gap between P* and the ceiling.

questions.topic: Binding price floor — quantity and surplus

source.label: Unit 4 Drill · Market A
source.note: Built on Market A from the Unit 4 slides (P = 100 − 2Q, P = 0.5Q). The slides show these policies on graphs; these calculations take them one step further, the way the Ch. 4 lesson page does.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. The government sets a **price floor of $30**. How many units are sold, and what does the floor create?
options: 60 units are sold, and there is a surplus of 25 units
35 units are sold, and there is a surplus (excess supply) of 25 units
35 units are sold, and there is a shortage of 25 units
40 units are sold, because the floor is not binding
questions.explanation: The floor ($30) is **above** P* ($20), so it binds. At $30, buyers want Q<sub>D</sub>: 30 = 100 − 2Q → **35**; sellers would offer Q<sub>S</sub>: 30 = 0.5Q → **60**. Buyers are now the short side, so only **35** are sold, leaving a **surplus of 60 − 35 = 25** unsold units. (a) counts what sellers *offer* as what is sold. A shortage (c) comes from a ceiling, not a floor ("Floor → Flood").

source.label: Unit 4 Drill · Market A
source.note: Built on Market A from the Unit 4 slides (P = 100 − 2Q, P = 0.5Q). The slides show these policies on graphs; these calculations take them one step further, the way the Ch. 4 lesson page does.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario (P* = $20, Q* = 40). Select **every** policy that would be **binding** — that is, would actually change the market outcome.
options: A price ceiling of $25
A price ceiling of $15
A price floor of $30
A price floor of $18
A quota of 50 units
A quota of 30 units
questions.explanation: The binding rules from the slides: a **ceiling binds only below P***, a **floor binds only above P***, and a **quota binds only below Q***. Otherwise *"it does not matter. The market will naturally trend towards P* (or Q*) anyway."* Ceiling $15 < $20 → **binding**; ceiling $25 → not. Floor $30 > $20 → **binding**; floor $18 → not. Quota 30 < 40 → **binding**; quota 50 → not. Memory aid: a floor holds prices **up**, so it only matters when it sits above P*; a ceiling holds prices **down**, so it only matters below P*.

source.label: Unit 4 Drill · Market A
source.note: Built on Market A from the Unit 4 slides (P = 100 − 2Q, P = 0.5Q). The slides show these policies on graphs; these calculations take them one step further, the way the Ch. 4 lesson page does.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. The government imposes a **quota of 30 units**. What price will buyers pay?
questions.explanation: With only 30 units available, the price is set by what buyers will pay for the 30th unit — read it off **demand**: P = 100 − 2(30) = **$40**. The quota is binding (30 < Q* = 40), so the price rises above P* = $20. Reading it off supply instead (0.5 × 30 = $15) gives the marginal cost of the last unit. The $25 gap between the two is the quota rent producers capture.

source.note: Built on Market A from the Unit 4 slides (P = 100 − 2Q, P = 0.5Q). The slides show these policies on graphs; these calculations take them one step further, the way the Ch. 4 lesson page does.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. A $15 ceiling, a $40 floor, a 30-unit quota and a $25 unit tax each cut Market A to 30 units, with the same $125 deadweight loss. Who ends up with the $750 rectangle, (40 − 15) × 30, under each policy?
options: Ceiling → producers; floor → consumers; quota → the government; tax → consumers
The government in every case
Ceiling → consumers; floor → producers; quota → producers; tax → the government
Nobody — it is part of the deadweight loss in every case
questions.explanation: The deadweight loss depends only on **which units are lost** (units 30–40), so it is $125 every time. The policies differ only in who gets the rectangle between the demand price ($40) and the supply price ($15) on the 30 units still traded. A **ceiling** holds the price at $15, so buyers keep it (PS → CS). A **floor** at $40 or a **quota** lets sellers charge $40 (CS → PS). A **tax** splits the prices at $40 / $15 and the government collects the gap as revenue. Rule of thumb: *the rectangle goes to whoever the policy was written for.* (d) confuses the rectangle (a transfer) with the triangle (a true loss).

source.label: Unit 4 Drill · Market A
source.note: Built on Market A from the Unit 4 slides (P = 100 − 2Q, P = 0.5Q). The slides show these policies on graphs; these calculations take them one step further, the way the Ch. 4 lesson page does.

questions.prompt: Refer to the scenario. The government pays producers a **$10 subsidy per unit**, so supply becomes P = 0.5Q − 10. What is the new outcome?
options: 44 units are traded; consumers pay $22 and producers receive $12 per unit
36 units are traded; consumers pay $28 per unit
40 units are traded; consumers pay $10 per unit
44 units are traded; consumers pay $12 and producers receive $22 per unit
questions.explanation: **Solve:** 0.5Q − 10 = 100 − 2Q → 2.5Q = 110 → **Q = 44** (up from 40). Consumers pay the **demand** price: 100 − 2(44) = **$12** (down $8). Producers receive the **original supply** price: 0.5(44) = **$22**, which is $12 from the buyer plus $10 from the government. The subsidy costs the government $10 × 44 = $440, which must be raised by taxing other goods (slide 11). (a) swaps the two prices. (b) treats the subsidy like a tax, shifting supply up instead of down.

questions.prompt: The government gives producers a per-unit subsidy. Draw the new supply curve S<sub>sub</sub>, then mark the new equilibrium E₂.

hints.shift: A subsidy lowers producers' cost per unit, so supply shifts DOWN (to the right) by the subsidy amount.

questions.explanation: A subsidy covers part of each unit's cost, so producers will supply every quantity at a price lower by the subsidy: **supply shifts down (right)**. Where S<sub>sub</sub> meets D, quantity is **higher** and the price consumers pay is **lower** than at E₁ (slide 11). Producers receive that consumer price **plus** the subsidy. This is the mirror image of the S + tax drill, which shifts supply up.

questions.prompt: The government imposes a binding quota. Draw the quota as the new supply limit (S<sub>quota</sub>), then mark the price buyers will pay at that quantity.

hints.slope: A quota caps quantity, so it is a VERTICAL line at the quota amount.
hints.shift: A binding quota must sit to the LEFT of Q* — a quota above Q* changes nothing.

tasks.label: P_Q
tasks.prompt: Mark the price buyers pay at the quota

questions.explanation: A quota is a **maximum quantity**, so supply becomes **vertical** at the quota (S<sub>quota</sub>, slide 42). To bind, it must sit **left of Q***. With only that many units available, buyers bid the price up to the **demand curve** at the quota, P<sub>Q</sub>, above P*. Consumer surplus is transferred to producers, and the units between the quota and Q* are a **deadweight loss** (slide 43).
